ta-l1d32q1-d1e100.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 32. Having treated the propers and appropriations of the persons, Lombard asks how the persons compare with one another by them: first by what is proper or appropriated to the Spirit (whether Father and Son love each other by the Holy Spirit), then by what is appropriated to the Son (whether the Father is wise by begotten or unbegotten wisdom), and finally of one person by comparison with another, a question he leaves unsolved as difficult. On the second he answers that the Son is not wise from begotten wisdom (efficiently) but is wise by it (formally), and removes the doubt whether the Father has only one wisdom, by the parallel of love, which is the whole Trinity, while the Spirit is a love that is not Father or Son. Thomas asks about what pertains to the Spirit and then to the Son. On the Spirit, three articles: whether the Father loves the Son by the Holy Spirit; whether the Father loves himself by the Holy Spirit; and whether Father and Son love us by the Holy Spirit.
claims: The ablative 'by wisdom' can express efficient or formal causality.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e137.summary: First argument that the Father does not love the Son by the Holy Spirit. As for God to be is to be wise, so to be is to love, and the Father is in no way said to be by the Holy Spirit.
claims: Loving is identical with being in God.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e140.summary: Second argument. The ablative must express some causal relation, efficient or formal, which can be expressed by a preposition, so the Father would love the Son 'from' or 'through' the Spirit, both false, since the Spirit has no character of principle with respect to the Father.
claims: The ablative resolves into a causal preposition.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e143.summary: Third argument. 'Loves' signifies an essential or notional act. If essential, any other essential act could replace it ('the Father lives by the Holy Spirit'), which is false; if notional, it signifies only common spiration, so 'the Father spirates the Spirit by the Spirit' would follow, which is false.
claims: Neither essential nor notional reading works.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e147.summary: Fourth argument. Every love by which people love each other is a bond uniting them, but the Spirit cannot unite Father and Son, since what unites has an influence on the united, producing the union.
claims: A uniting bond influences the united.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e150.summary: Sed contra, Hugh of St Victor's argument. As a man's love proceeds from him, the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son as love, and a man loves another by the love proceeding from him, so the Father loves the Son by the Spirit.
claims: One loves by the love proceeding from oneself.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e153.summary: Second sed contra. By every perfect love someone loves and someone is loved, and the Spirit is perfect love, which can only be of Father and Son.
claims: Perfect love has lover and beloved.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e156.summary: Thomas's determination. There are many opinions. Some say all such locutions are false, retracted by Augustine in the parallel case of the Father wise by begotten wisdom; but Augustine named what he retracted and retracted only his own sayings, and since he and all others use such locutions, denying them seems presumptuous. Others say they are true but improper, meaning 'by essential love appropriated to the Spirit', but then the Father could be called wise by the Son, i.e. essential wisdom appropriated to the Son. Others hold them true and proper, variously: some resolve the ablative into 'through', implying subauthority in the Spirit as when the Father works through the Son, but 'through' designates causality in the one it is joined to with respect to the effect, and here there is no effect of which the Spirit is principle; some take the ablative as sign and quasi-effect, the Spirit being a sign that Father and Son love each other, but created love is such a sign too, and the Spirit is the Father's love, by which one loves formally; others take it as form, since they love formally by the love that is the Spirit, but a form denominates only by inhering, and the Spirit is subsistent, not inhering, and every form is a principle of what it informs, making the Spirit a principle of something in the Father. So others, apparently following Hugh of St Victor, take it as a quasi-formal effect, 'effect' broadly meaning whatever is from a principle and 'formal' meaning what has the act of form in denominating: the love that is the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son, by which they love each other. This combines the last two views and should be accepted. To explain: the mode of denomination varies by genus. Some genera, like quality and quantity, signify as inhering and denominate only by an inherent form. Others signify as from another, not as inhering, chiefly action, which as action is signified as from the agent, its being in the agent belonging to it as an accident; so in the genus of action something is denominated by what is from it, not by its principle, as one acts by action, though action is not the agent's principle. If there were an action that was not an accident, it would denominate the agent without inhering. Since every action has an inherent form as principle, something is called agent either by the action itself or by the form that is its principle, as fire moves upward by its proper motion and by lightness. 'To love' in God is said essentially, implying only conceptual procession, or notionally, implying the real procession of love from lover, and in each way love is said as quality (the habit in the lover) or as operation (the act). Essentially, the Father loves the Son denominatively by love as essential act and by its principle, charity, the divine substance. Notionally, if love means the form that is principle of the act, the Father loves by the property that is principle of the Spirit's procession, as paternity of generation; if it means the proceeding action itself, the Father loves the Son by the love that is the Spirit, or by the Holy Spirit. Likewise with other personal names signifying the person by way of operation, like 'Word', so the Father speaks by his Word.
claims: 'The Father loves the Son by the Holy Spirit' is true and proper, the ablative signifying a quasi-formal effect, as one acts by one's action.
In the genus of action something is denominated by what proceeds from it, not only by an inhering form.
Notionally the Father loves by the Spirit as proceeding operation, as he speaks by the Word.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e159.summary: Reply to the first argument. To love taken essentially is entirely the same as to be, in reality and in mode of signifying, which is absolute, so in that sense the Father does not love by the Spirit. Taken notionally, it differs from being in mode of signifying, since it is said relatively, so it does not follow that he is by the Spirit though he loves by the Spirit, as he is Father by paternity but not by paternity is. 'To be wise' in God is always essential, so the Father is in no way wise by begotten wisdom.
claims: Notional loving differs from being in mode of signifying; being wise is always essential.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e162.summary: Reply to the second argument. Personal love relates to the loving Father not as principle of love but as denominating act, so the ablative expresses no principle, nor form as principle, but form only as denominating, as 'he acts by action'. Since prepositions explicitly imply causal relation, 'the Father loves the Son through the Spirit' is less proper than 'by the Spirit', though it may be granted as principle of denomination, not simply; 'from the Spirit' must in no way be granted, since it says efficient principle.
claims: 'By the Spirit' is proper; 'through' only qualifiedly; 'from' not at all.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e166.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'Loves' signifies a notional act, which includes the act itself and the act's going out from the agent. The act itself is the person of the Spirit; its emanation is properly the notion or notional act, procession. So the Spirit is signified not by the verb, which signifies the act as going out from the agent, but by a noun signifying the act absolutely, 'love' or 'dilection'. 'To love' properly says a notion, meaning 'to emit love', and so includes the act itself, the person, by which the Father is denominated loving by love, the Spirit, and the emission, which makes it notional. 'Spirates' signifies only the emission, not the emitted act, so the Father is not called spirating by the Spirit but by the act or property of spiration. Likewise generation says emission of the begotten, so the Father does not beget by the Word, but 'to speak' says both emission and the emitted Word, so he speaks by the Word. 'Word' names what is emitted, so it is personal like 'love', while 'to love' is notional like 'to speak'.
claims: 'Diligere' and 'dicere' include both emission and the emitted person; 'spirare' and 'generare' only the emission.
So the Father loves by the Spirit and speaks by the Word, but does not spirate by the Spirit or beget by the Son.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e169.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. 'Father and Son are united by the Spirit' is true, as the Spirit is the union itself, the love by which they are formally united, and as what proceeds from them, as several are united by one act. But 'the Spirit unites Father and Son' should not be granted simply, since 'unite' signifies uniting efficiently, which does not fit the Spirit, though it can be granted of uniting formally, as whiteness makes white.
claims: Father and Son are united by the Spirit formally, not efficiently.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e181.summary: First argument that the Father does not love himself by the Spirit. If 'love' is essential, it is common and signifies the essence; if notional, no notional act reflects on its source, as the Father does not beget himself.
claims: Notional acts do not reflect on their source.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e184.summary: Second argument. The Spirit's procession presupposes the Son's generation by order of nature, and whatever belongs to the Father by himself can belong to him without the generation being understood, so if the Father loved himself by the Spirit, the Spirit would proceed from the Father as love even without the Son.
claims: Self-love would not presuppose the Son.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e187.summary: Third argument. Gratuitous love always tends to another (Gregory: charity requires at least two), and created charity is modelled on uncreated charity, the Spirit, so the Father's self-love is not the personal love.
claims: Charity requires two.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e191.summary: Fourth argument. By whatever love the Father loves himself, Son and Spirit love themselves, so the Spirit would love himself by the Spirit, and since love proceeds from the lover, the Spirit would proceed from himself.
claims: The Spirit would proceed from himself.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e194.summary: Sed contra. The Father loves the Son and himself by the same love, and he loves the Son by the Spirit.
claims: One love for Son and self.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e197.summary: Second sed contra. As love is proper to the Spirit, Word is proper to the Son, and the Father speaks himself by the Word (Anselm), so he loves himself by the love proceeding from him, the Spirit.
claims: The Father speaks himself by the Word.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e200.summary: Thomas's determination. Essentially, the Father loves himself, like the Son, not by the Spirit but by essential charity and operation. Notionally, he loves himself by the Spirit as he loves the Son, since notional loving is being the principle of the personal love, the Spirit, which as operation denominates the Father it is from. Since the whole character of lovability in the Son is in the Father and conversely, nothing prevents the Father from loving himself by the Spirit, neither on the side of the spirator, since the Father is a sufficient principle of the Spirit, nor on the side of the lovable, which is sufficiently in him and the Spirit. So the Father loves himself and the Spirit by the Spirit, as he loves the Son.
claims: Notionally the Father loves himself and the Spirit by the Spirit, as he loves the Son.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e203.summary: Reply to the first argument. It is understood of the notional act. Every notional act implies a principle of origin, either with respect to its terminus, as 'the Father begets the Son', where no reflexive is possible since no person is its own principle, or not with respect to what the act passes into, as 'the Father gives the essence to the Son', where he is principle of the recipient, not of what is given. 'To love' implies the principle of the lover to the love, not to the beloved, so reflexive use is possible, because the verb includes not only emission but the emitted love itself; taken separately as to origin only there is no reflexive, since the Father does not spirate himself.
claims: 'Diligere' implies principle with respect to the love emitted, not the beloved, so it can be reflexive.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e206.summary: Reply to the second argument. If there were no generation of the Son, the Father would not love himself by the Spirit, since he would not be Father, his person being constituted by paternity. If, per impossibile, the Father's person remained, he could spirate personal love by himself, yet the Son is not excluded from this, since every perfection of the Father in which they are not relatively opposed is the Son's too.
claims: Without generation there would be no Father; spirative perfection is shared with the Son.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e210.summary: Reply to the third argument. Gratuitous love is not a private love, and it tends to another, yet it also reflects on the lover, since one must love by charity not only one's neighbour but oneself in soul and body; so the Father too loves himself by the Spirit.
claims: Charity includes self-love.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e213.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. 'The Spirit loves himself by the Spirit' is plainly true of essential love, since as God is by himself he is essentially loving by himself. Of notional love, 'to love' includes a twofold act, the act of love signifying the Spirit and the emission of love, so notional loving is spirating love, as begetting is begetting a son, and as the Son does not beget a son, the Spirit does not spirate love, with no imperfection (Dist. 7), so in this sense the Spirit does not love notionally. If the act of origin is separated from 'loves', leaving only what is personal, the love itself, it would fit the Spirit, who proceeds as subsistent operation, the operation itself operating, and then the Spirit would love himself or the Father by himself, 'loving' implying only the person differently signified. So 'to love' is taken in three ways: essentially, a conceptual going out of essential operation, by which no person loves by the Spirit; as naming only the person of the Spirit, so only the Spirit loves, an unusual usage; or as real going out, implying the active notion and the Spirit, and so only Father and Son love.
claims: 'Diligere' can be essential, merely personal (unusual), or notional (only Father and Son).
The Spirit does not love notionally, without imperfection.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e225.summary: First argument that Father and Son do not love us by the Spirit. Every name connoting an effect in creatures is essential, and God's love for creatures connotes its effect, so it is essential, and in the essential sense no one loves by the Spirit.
claims: Love of creatures is essential.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e228.summary: Second argument. On Hugh's view the ablative expresses a quasi-formal effect, but in the comparison of God to creatures the Spirit is not effect but rather what is effected in the creature.
claims: The Spirit is not an effect relative to creatures.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e231.summary: Third argument. Love relates to the Spirit as generation to the Son, and the Father does not beget us by the Son but rather regenerates us by the Spirit.
claims: The Father does not beget us by the Son.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e235.summary: Sed contra from John 17:22, 'that they may be one in us, as we are one', which concerns not essential unity, by which we are not united to God, but the unity of consonance or love, the Holy Spirit.
claims: We are united in the love that is the Spirit.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e241.summary: Second sed contra. As Word is proper to the Son, love is proper to the Spirit, and the Father speaks every creature by his Word (Augustine: he begot the Word in whom it was that they be made), so he loves creatures by his love, the Spirit.
claims: The Father speaks creatures by the Word.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e247.summary: Thomas's determination. Father and Son love us by the Holy Spirit, as Dist. 10 says. The procession of the divine persons is a kind of origin of the procession of creatures, since the first in any genus causes what follows, though efficiency over creatures is attributed to the common essence. 'To love' here can be taken essentially or notionally, and either way the locution is true. Essentially, the verb designates the efficiency of the whole Trinity, and the ablative designating the Spirit designates the reason of efficiency on the side of the effects, whose reason and origin is the Spirit's procession, as also the Word's; but the Word is properly the reason of creatures as they go out from God by way of intellect, so the Father speaks all things by his Word or art, while the Spirit is their reason as they go out by freedom of will, so God properly loves creatures by the Spirit, not by the Word. Notionally, it is true by another reason: the verb does not principally imply efficiency toward creatures but the reason of this efficiency on the side of the effects, and consequently gives to understand efficiency (Dist. 30): the Father loves creatures by the Spirit, i.e. spirates the personal love that is the reason of every free gift of God to creatures.
claims: Father and Son love us by the Spirit, essentially and notionally.
The Spirit's procession is the reason of creatures' going out by free will, as the Word is of their going out by intellect.
concepts: Spirit as reason of free giving

ta-l1d32q1-d1e250.summary: Reply to the first argument. It can be taken either way. Essentially, nothing unfitting follows, since the Spirit designates the principle not of the lovers but of the loved, the ablative's relation being in the ablative itself (Praepositinus). Notionally, the nominative can connote an effect in creatures by way of relation to the term (Dist. 30).
claims: Essentially the Spirit designates the reason on the side of the beloved.

ta-l1d32q1-d1e253.summary: Reply to the second argument. In the going out of artefacts from art there are two processes, of the art from the artisan who devises it, and of the artefacts from the art; so in the process of will there are the going out of love from the lover and of the thing given through love from love. As to the first, the Spirit relates, in God's comparison to creatures, as effect or what is from a principle, like the Word; as to the second, Word and Love both are principle, and the creature is effect.
claims: The Spirit is quasi-effect as proceeding from the lover and principle as source of gifts.
concepts: two processes in art and will

ta-l1d32q1-d1e256.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'Begets' implies only the origin of the person, not the person by way of act, as 'love' and 'speak' do, so the Father is not denominated begetting by the Son but by generation, while he is denominated loving by the love that is the Spirit. Our regeneration is not by nature but by will, so on our side the Spirit, rather than the Son, who proceeds by nature, is its reason.
claims: Regeneration is by will, so its reason is the Spirit.

ta-l1d32q1-Dd1e92.summary: The opening section of Distinction 32 divides Lombard's comparison of the persons by propers and appropriations: whether Father and Son love by the Spirit, whether the Father is wise by begotten wisdom, and a question left unsolved. It announces three articles on what pertains to the Spirit.
claims: The ablative of wisdom can be efficient or formal.

ta-l1d32q1-Dd1e129.summary: Article 1 holds that 'the Father loves the Son by the Holy Spirit' is true and proper. After rejecting readings of it as false, improper, subauthoritative, sign-based, or formal, Thomas follows Hugh of St Victor: the ablative signifies a quasi-formal effect, since in the genus of action something is denominated by what proceeds from it. Notionally the Father loves by the Spirit as proceeding operation, as he speaks by the Word, while 'diligere' and 'dicere' include the emitted person and 'spirare' and 'generare' do not. Father and Son are united by the Spirit formally, not efficiently.
claims: The Father loves the Son by the Spirit as by a proceeding operation that denominates him.
He loves and speaks by Spirit and Word but does not spirate by the Spirit or beget by the Son.

ta-l1d32q1-Dd1e173.summary: Article 2 holds that notionally the Father loves himself and the Spirit by the Spirit, as he loves the Son, since the character of lovability and the sufficiency of principle are in him. 'Diligere' can be reflexive because it implies principle toward the emitted love, not the beloved. Charity includes self-love, and 'diligere' has three senses (essential, merely personal, notional), so the Spirit does not love notionally, without imperfection.
claims: Notionally the Father loves himself by the Spirit.
The Spirit does not love notionally.

ta-l1d32q1-Dd1e217.summary: Article 3 holds that Father and Son love us by the Spirit, essentially and notionally, since the Spirit's procession is the reason of creatures' going out by free will, as the Word is of their going out by intellect. The Spirit is quasi-effect as proceeding from the lover and principle of gifts, and our regeneration is by will, so its reason is the Spirit.
claims: Father and Son love creatures by the Spirit, the reason of every free gift.
concepts: Spirit as reason of free giving

ta-l1d32q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 32 treats locutions pertaining to the Spirit. Article 1 holds, with Hugh of St Victor, that the Father loves the Son by the Spirit, the ablative signifying a quasi-formal effect, as one acts by one's action, so the Father loves and speaks by the persons proceeding as operations. Article 2 holds that notionally the Father loves himself by the Spirit too, while the Spirit does not love notionally. Article 3 holds that Father and Son love us by the Spirit, whose procession is the reason of creatures' free going out and of every gift.
claims: The Father loves the Son, himself, and us by the Spirit, as by a proceeding operation.
The Spirit's procession is the reason of creatures' free going out.
